# The Seafarer Class

*Pages PDF 63-79*

## **The Seafarer Class**
## **A Set of Careers Closely Associated with the Sea and Seafaring**
The Seafarer Class is a new Class for use in **Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay** , representing Careers pursued by people who live around the coasts of the Old World. There is much in common between the Seafarer Class and the Riverfolk Class, and certain Careers belong to both Classes, such as Huffer, Seaman, and Wrecker. 

The table on this page is designed to replace the Riverfolk section of the Random Class and Career Table on page 30 and 31 of the **WFRP Core Rulebook** . The player generating the career must choose whether they want to substitute the Seafarers for the Riverfolk before rolling on the table. 

Riverfolk careers that possess the Lore (Riverways) Skill may substitute it for the Lore (Oceans) Skill. There are still many small-scale seafaring folk who follow the lifestyle of Boatmen, Riverwomen, or Smugglers, after all. 

## **Class Trappings**
**Seafarers:** Cloak, Clothing, Dagger, Pouch, Sling Bag containing a 10 yard length of rope and a Flask of Spirits 

## **New Talents**
## **Chanty**
**Max:** Intelligence Bonus 

**Tests** : Entertain (Singing) 

This Talent allows a Character to learn a chanty (see page 67). Whenever a Character buys a new level in the Talent they learn a new song. A Chanty affects an entire crew. To use the talent the Chantyman should find a location within earshot of as many of the crew as possible and pass an Entertain (Singing) Test. 

It takes 30 seconds for a Chantyman to establish the chanty, after which the effect lasts for three minutes plus a number of minutes equal to the SL on the Entertain (Singing) Test. The only combat action the Chantyman can make while the Chanty is being performed is a Dodge. Other actions can be made at the GM’s discretion, such as Perception Tests or Cool Tests. If the Chantyman takes damage or fails any Opposed Test their Chanty ends. 

A Chanty may be sung at each watch. There’s only so much inspiration a crew can take.

## **Crew Commander**
**Max:** Initiative Bonus 

**Tests** : Ranged Skill Tests when firing a weapon with the Crewed Flaw 

A Character with this Talent is practised at managing crews of siege weapons and artillery pieces. The Character may make a **Challenging (+0) Leadership** Test to help a crew operating a weapon with the Crewed Flaw within earshot. If the Character passes the Test, the crew members may then use the Character’s Ranged Skill when shooting the weapon. 

## **Master and Commander**
## **Max** : Fellowship Bonus **Tests** : Leadership
You are respected and trusted by your crew. Any appropriate Leadership Test on board your ship or involving your crew gains an SL bonus equal to your levels in Master and Commander. This bonus applies to Crew Tests as well as individual Leadership Tests. 

## **Beachcomber**
Halfling, Human 

_You scour the local beaches for anything of value, always on the lookout for a hidden gem or lucky find._ 

Beachcombers live by their wits upon the littoral, finding most of what they need to survive through Manann’s providence. A diverse range of flotsam and jetsam gets washed up on the beaches of the Sea of Claws, and Beachcombers take full advantage of this. Almost any item that can be traded will find itself aboard a ship on the Sea of Claws, and therefore, provided it floats for a time, could end up washed up on a beach. Such castaway cargo can often fetch good money from a local merchant or be bartered for other useful stuff. 

_‘Fifteen years I’ve been patrolling this beach and I never dreamt of finding anything as valuable as a ball of ambergris. And my dream came true: I never found anything as valuable as a ball of ambergris.’_ — Mad Janie, Beachcomber 

_‘I found a boot last year, lovely it was, all fur lined. After I dried it out, I gave it to a farmer, special offer, buy one get one free. I’m still looking for the other one.’_ 

— Mad Janie, Beachcomber

## **Master of the Beach – Silver 2**
**Skills:** Leadership, Trade (Boatbuilder)

**Talents:** Dealmaker, River Guide, Seasoned Traveller, Tenacious

**Trappings:** Wreck Dwelling 

Beachcombers consider their ‘patch’ their own territory and guard it jealously. They will fight to keep others out. Gangs of Beachcombers will band together to defend their patches or encroach upon others’. 

Beachcombers aren’t just after flotsam and jetsam; they also look out for more naturally-occurring plants and creatures. They collect all kinds of shellfish, anemones, and even sea slugs, knowing the best locations to find them, and they are expert at identifying the tastiest — or less inedible — ones. The best shells can be sold to local merchants, and once they find their way to big inland cities, like Nuln or Altdorf, they can fetch a high price. 

## **The Bounty of the Beach**
Amber also sells for a good price, and while it is seen as a bit old-fashioned in the Empire, is still much sought after in Norsca. All Beachcombers live in hope of finding a piece of ambergris, which is highly valuable as it is used as the basis for the finest perfumes for the nobles of Bretonnia. 

Beachcombers have excellent knowledge of their beaches and know how to avoid hazards like quicksand and treacherous tides. They are also known for accurately forecasting the weather. The best time to search is as the tide turns, so Beachcombers have as good a knowledge of tide times as anyone. They also know the comings and goings of local sea traffic. 

With their constant, seemingly innocent presence on the seafront, and their knowledge of tides, currents, and the local shipping patterns, Beachcombers are useful to local pirates and wreckers, and are often roped in to help them. For similar reasons they are often consulted by the local authorities, too. 

Beachcombers usually end up living close to the shoreline so they can be around as the tide turns. Used to the harsh environment, they can make their homes in cliffside shacks, or even caves within the cliffs themselves. They can also be found — and it is a point of pride among Beachcombers to occupy such a desirable residence — living within wrecked or grounded hulks. 

## The Seaweed Man
Among the Beachcombers of the Sea of Claws, and among those they talk to, the story of the Seaweed Man is well known. Tales tell of a hulking figure, eight or nine feet tall, that shambles across the beach at dawn and dusk. It seems to be composed of seaweed, shells, tentacles, and other detritus. 

Though the creature lumbers on dry ground, in the water it swims as fast as any fish, and if ever spotted, disappears into the depths as fast as it appears, leaving little trace save indistinct tracks across the sand. If a Beachcomber ever goes missing, it is because the Seaweed Man got them. 

## The Receiver of Wrecks
The Imperial government accommodates the office of ‘The Emperor’s Official Receiver of Wrecks and Derelicts’. Housed far from the sea in Altdorf, the Receiver of Wrecks is charged with recording the site of every shipwreck in Imperial waters. It also, technically, owns these wrecks and anything found upon them, though it does offer a reward of one crown in ten for any salvage reported to it. 

It is the responsibility of every ship’s captain to inform this office if their ship should go down, and it is the responsibility of anyone finding a wreck, or flotsam, jetsam, or anything else, to report their finds. The office is not as busy as it should be. 

## **Chantyman**
## High Elf, Human
_You coordinate the actions of your ship’s crew, guide their activity, and raise their morale with rousing ditties._ 

Any sailor worth their salt performs better to the sound of a Chantyman. Some say they are just singers and musicians, like any others. However, it is a common belief amongst most ship’s crews that the best Chantymen can have an unnatural effect upon the crew.

_‘It was my first day aboard, I didn’t know whether I was coming or going. I felt like I couldn’t keep up with the rest of the crew. But then the fiddle started playing, and he started singing, and it suddenly all fitted together.’_ — Marian Zelman, Seaman 

The Chantyman is a member of the crew of a boat, usually an ocean-going vessel, who sings songs to lift the mood of the crew, to keep time and coordinate their activities, and to spur them on to greater effort. Nearly all ships will have someone who performs this task, but not all will have a genuine Chantyman. 

The Chantyman is special in that their songs have a power that will lift the crew beyond what mundane means can accomplish. Even if the crew is unaware of such powers, they might have a feeling that their Chantyman really does stir their soul and spur them on. Most Chantymen will accompany themselves with a musical instrument, all the better for keeping good time and making themselves heard above the racket of a working ship. They can, however, work without one. 

## **Chanties and Manann**
The Chantyman is inextricably linked with the worship of Manann. It is clear that Manann likes a good song, what with the sound of the wind skipping over the water, the crash of the waves, and the rumble of the sea. There are many songs sung about the sea or on the sea by any number of people. These are often called chanties, too, but they are not the special songs sung by Chantymen that seem to attract Manann’s favour. 

## Gods of the Several Seas
It is assumed here that chanties are associated with Manann, and the Chantyman is devoted to that god. This is appropriate for Humans on the Sea of Claws, but other gods might inspire Chantymen, too. The Elven worship of Mathlann is an obvious candidate, whether it is an aspect of Manann or a separate god. 

The debate as to whether other sea gods from around the world are all essentially a single entity or separate gods, is endlessly debated in the finest academic establishments and the cloisters of religious institutions around the globe. While no definitive answer has been forthcoming, it is clear that cultures that do not worship the name of Manann have singers and musicians who inspire their seafarers. 

Perhaps even Stromfels might inspire Chantymen — but not, of course, those darker gods whose power manifests in significantly more unsavoury ways. 

## **List of Chanties**
Chanties are not individual feats of worship and no divine power manifests when they occur. They are low-key, and require the participation, however passive, of a ship’s crew to work. A Chantyman need not understand or believe in any metaphysical process behind his song, but they must sing with gusto and sincerity to have an effect. 

## **We’re All in This Together So, Heave Ho, Heave Ho…**
This Chanty will spread a spirit of cooperation and make the crew knuckle down and go about the running of the ship with vigour and confidence. It gives a +10 modifier to the individual Tests of every crew member involved in any Crew Test. 

## **Jacques Bret Came Sailing to Meet Our Steel!**
This rousing Chanty tells of heroic feats in bloody battles. It pumps the blood of the crew and stirs them for the fight. It gives everyone in the crew +1 SL on any successful Melee Test. 

## **Of All the Terrors Upon the Sea…**
This steady, heart-warming melody can steel the hearts of a wavering crew. It gives them +1 SL to Cool Tests. 

## **You Band of Shipmates Gather Round…**
This is a round that encourages others to join in, and its gentle tempo and lyrics induce calm. It gives anyone in the crew +1 SL to any Fellowship Test intended to befriend or placate other members of the crew. 

## **All Arise, for the Night Has Eyes…**
This Chanty is a soft melodic one, but the words have an implicit warning. It is usually sung at night; it helps make everyone on board the ship calm and restful but keeps those on watch alert. Anyone trying to remain awake gets +20 on any Test that might result in them falling asleep, and they also get +10 to any Perception Test. 

## **The Ladies of L’anguille…**
This bawdy song has countless verses, and sailors are encouraged to add their own to the risqué litany. This is designed to amuse and lift morale. Anyone joining in the song can ignore one Condition. 

## **They Do Say Do as the Captain Do Say…**
This song about the many heroic deeds of the fictional Captain Vriez Van Vijnen instils a sense of optimism and trust in the ship’s captain. Any Fellowship Test attempted by the Captain, or other authority figure on board, targeted at the crew, gets a +20 bonus. 

## **Huffer**
## Dwarf, Halfling, High Elf, Human
_You guide ships through the most treacherous waters of the world’s several seas._ 

Huffers are known to work on the rivers of the Empire, but pilots and navigators are obviously even more invaluable to captains of ocean-going vessels. Not only is knowledge of areas of rock, reef, or sandbank necessary, but seafarers often sail beyond sight of any landmark, so navigators at sea must display practical knowledge of how to pinpoint their location from the position of the sun and the stars.

## **Master Pilot — Silver 5**
**Skills:** Leadership, Sail

**Talents:** Sharp, Sixth Sense, Strong Swimmer, Tenacious

**Trappings:** Boathand, Small Boat

_‘We call that one Ironhard Snorri, for in the year 2849 of our calendar, it split the Grubark of Buri Foambeard from bow to stern and only by the mercy of Valaya were all hands spared. That one behind it is Treacherous Norn, responsible for dashing the brains from the head of Thuri Thingolsson when he fell overboard in the gales of ‘82. That one there, may Grungni see that it is never so much as chipped, is Friendly Olaf, for the dragonship of the hated Haftur Aesling was smashed into matchwood upon its limpet-chewed flanks.’_ — Grum Grumsson of Kraka Ravnsvake identifies the rocks at the mouth of the Dypvann 

The Sea of Claws is a treacherous place. The coastlines of Nordland and Ostland are known for their rocky shores, and the coast of Norsca is a maze of inlets and islands. No serious captain expects to complete their voyage without the assistance of a local pilot who can show them how to approach the shore without striking a rock. 

Further west, the pilots who work around the coastline of L’Anguille are particularly famed, for the many rocks of the Dragon’s Maw present the most challenging hazard in the sea, a vast swathe of ocean pierced by hundreds upon hundreds of jutting spires of rock. 

Most settlements around the sea are home to a few individuals who can help guide ships safely to harbour. They may work for a fee paid by the captains of visiting ships, or in some cases even be paid a salary raised by their home community, who recognise that by providing the service they can help attract trade. 

## **The Dwarf Book of Charts**
Whilst the Elves, Norse, and Bretonnians are all renowned for their skill as sailors, it may come as a surprise to learn that some of the greatest pilots and navigators in the world are Dwarfs, for they are not famed as great mariners in the way that Humans and Elves are. 

The reason for their expertise is partly down to the nature of the Dwarf psyche, for the possession of a good memory, particularly where a grievance is concerned, can prove valuable in assisting a pilot to remain mindful of hazards. Those who know Dwarfs are sometimes heard to joke that the navigators of Kraka Ravnsvake and Barak Varr must keep records of grudges towards every spur of rock and branch of coral that ever so much as scratched the hull of an Ironclad. 

The truth is not so far off, for the other reason Dwarfs make good navigators is cultural. The naval arm of the Dwarf Engineers’ Guild compile and update a great lexicon of lore called _The Book of Charts_ . These ironbound compendiums of maps and sealore are written in secret glyphs and passed among members of the Guild and the Dwarf navy. 

## **Hazards Around the Sea of Claws**
_‘You seem to have become stuck? By all of the gods, I have guided Knarr and Longship through these fjords all of my life and never has a ship that followed me been troubled. The waters here are as deep as a Troll is tall. How is it that your vessel is impeded?’_ — Norse Pilot Ivar Knutsson learns what a keel is 

Pilots and navigators around the Sea of Claws know to be wary of certain areas. The easiest approach to take to dangerous stretches of coastline is to avoid them, but rare pilots make a special effort (and take tremendous risks) to learn how to navigate them. These pilots are then able to offer a rare and exclusive service to those ships desperate enough to wish to travel such waters. 

The Dragon’s Maw to the north of L’Anguille is the most notorious of these sites, but not the only one. Ships sailing from Marienburg typically head far out to sea before changing their bearing, doing so to avoid Reavers Point, a penninsula to the north of the Wasteland famed for its treacherous rocks, and the treacherous wreckers who scavenge from any vessel that becomes stricken there. 

Further east, along the coast to the north of the Laurelorn Forest, the seas are plagued by a tribe of Goblins known as the Reavaz. This tribe are noted for their blue-green skins and seafaring skill. They have been said to inhabit the area ever since the invasion of Grom the Paunch. The Eonir claim to hunt them down with malice, and flotillas of their ramshackle craft are often destroyed by Nordlander warships, but they remain a stubborn presence in the many caves that riddle the cliffsides. 

The Skeer, west of Salkalten, is an area of jagged rocks on the Ostland coast, and another haunt of wreckers. 

Pilots who can navigate such areas reliably are masters of their craft, even without leaving the coasts around what is considered the safer, civilised, lands to the south of the Sea of Claws. Those with knowledge of the Troll Country’s bleak coasts, or the icy fjords of Norsca, are rarer still. 

Many Dwarf pilots and navigators have made a study of this work, and benefit greatly from the accumulated knowledge therein. 

## **Officer**
Dwarf, High Elf, Human 

_You command a ship, and must inspire your crew to place their lives in your hands._ 

Ship’s Officers, especially captains, are judge, jury, and executioner aboard their vessels. They have Mananngiven power of life and death over the crew, but this is a double-edged sword. The Officer must also inspire the crew to trust their judgement and competence, or the hands might mutiny. 

_‘She was a brutal sort, had me flogged a couple of times, but I was glad to have her as my captain when the ship hit the Fang. Would never have made it off alive. May she rest in peace.’_ — Marian Zelman, Seaman 

_‘What a captain he was, had the finest uniform I ever saw, gold braid everywhere. He had the shiniest shoes and the blackest hat with the biggest feather you’ve ever seen. The ship was run like a Shallyan orphanage, mind.’_ — Marian Zelman, Seaman

**Trappings:** A Fleet

Imperial Navy Officers often come from sea-faring families. These are often minor noble houses or aspiring gentry with a tradition of service at sea. The potential Officer will often be groomed from a young age with the expectation that they are to go to sea to seek their fortune. Whilst nepotism is rife in the Imperial First Fleet, in many other navies an Officer must work their way up from a humble midshipman. Life on board ship demands competence and respect, and Officers must be seen to have done their time and learned their craft. 

Discipline aboard ship is paramount, and the cruel and arbitrary captain is a common archetype among the seafarers of the Sea of Claws, but most sailors know that their safety is entwined with their captain’s if only because, should the worst happen, the captain must be prepared to go down with their ship. 

## **Recognition of Merit**
It is not uncommon for an Officer to make their way up from another career. Common seamen and others can become midshipmen and rise from there. These are usually given more respect by the crew than a young noble straight from school, for example, but might need to work harder to show their qualities to more privileged Officers and captains. 

It is the ambition of any Officer to become a captain and command their own vessel. While trappings in WFRP are often negotiable or merely suggestions, it would be very difficult indeed for a third-tier Officer to claim to be a captain if they had no vessel to command. 

## Bounty
Finding and salvaging a wreck or taking a prize in battle can be very lucrative to a ship’s crew, and many a deck hand has dreamt of the day that they might be fortunate enough to come across a stricken vessel with a rich cargo. Such bounty is distributed strictly according to a well-established system of shares. 

While a brand-new powder monkey might only have the right to one share, an experienced captain could have as many as a hundred. Every promotion and every few years of service gains a crewmember an extra share. In practice, however, a crewmember might go their entire life without a sniff of even the smallest prize. But if a crew does earn itself a sizeable bounty, these shares are jealously monitored and discussed in every corner of the ship. Real or imagined unfairness in this regard has been the cause of many a fight. 

## The Captain’s Log
One of the less appreciated jobs of the captain is to keep a log of their voyage. This should be detailed and meticulous to enable any reader to understand as much about the voyage as possible. This can be vital to recreating the journey, or understanding why a ship was lost, or why a voyage went wrong, and is important for insurance purposes, too. 

Many captains take great care in their logs; others see it as a tedious chore to get over with as quickly as possible. Of course, it’s not unknown for a captain to use this record  to talk up their role in a successful voyage or play down their mistakes in a disastrous one. 

## The Bretonnian Admiralty
The Imperial Sea Lords have a reputation for nepotism and aristocratic snobbery. Merit takes a marked second place to lineage when it comes to advancement within their ranks. However, at least they can be said to be sailors. The Bretonnian Admiralty, in contrast, are selected mostly on the basis of who has best impressed the King and the Grand Dukes of that land. Not only does this mean that common sailors can never expect to be raised to the ranks of the admiralty, but that those noblefolk who are often know more about hosting lavish tournaments, feasts, and balls than they do about sailing. 

Despite this the Bretonnians are thought great seafarers. It is an open secret within the Bretonnian navy that the officers tend to delegate the management of their vessels to captains who cut their teeth as buccaneers, though to say so out loud would be to earn a taste of the nine-tailed cat. 

## **Sailor**
Dwarf, Halfling, High Elf, Human 

_You work on board a ship, keeping the decks clean and the sails suitably trimmed._ 

Humans of the Old World had to learn the skills of sailing for themselves, for the Dwarfs were never a great maritime civilisation, and the Elves had no desire to encourage Human exploration of the wider world. Human civilisation before the age of Sigmar rarely ventured upon the waves. Even the mighty Khemrians built few vessels capable of ocean travel. 

Yet once the rudiments of catching the wind and navigating by sun and stars were learned, the Humans of the Old World grew to be confident and competent sailors. Now many Old World nations boast fine seafaring traditions. 

_‘Call me Marian. I know better than most that the ocean is perilous and the storm terrible, but I have never found such dangers sufficient reason for remaining aport, particularly if that port is Brionne.’_ — Marian Zelman, Seaman

## **Estalian Sailors**
The sailors of the southern realms are often cited as some of the best in the Old World. The Estalians in particular are noted as being particularly zealous in their hatred and prosecution of pirates. 

Many Estalian seamen have served on the blockade of the seas around the Bay of Quietude and trading port of Magritta, and have fought against smuggling crews and buccaneers. They make consummate sailors and are often chosen to lead boarding parties. They command high prices to serve on foreign ships, for whilst the Estalian kingdoms are fractious and disorganised, the natives of the country are noted for having a great deal of loyalty to their land and neighbours. 

## **Tilean Sailors**
Tilean sailors, in comparison, share many of the values held by the numerous mercenary companies who originate from that land. They are often found among the crews of foreign vessels and some have even risen to prominence as captains of Bretonnian ships. They have a great rivalry with the sailors of Estalia and many Tileans take a lax view of piracy, seeing little difference between the life of the mercenary and the life of the pirate. 

It is sometimes said in the northern realms that all Tilean sailors are pirates, but this is only true of those from Sartosa. It ought to be noted that whilst many Tileans are unconcerned about piracy, the sailors of Luccini and Remas are as set against it as those of Magritta. 

## **Bretonnian Sailors**
The Bretonnians also boast of a fine naval tradition. Their mighty galleons are on the cutting edge of naval technology, and the aversion to military innovation that has become enshrined elsewhere in the Bretonnian armed forces does not seem present on board its vessels. The Bretonnian Grand Admiralty is as hidebound as the rest of the kingdom’s institutions, however, being a club for gentlemen officers who rarely concern themselves with the welfare of the common sailor. 

The majestic vessels of the fleet are often bolstered by a number of small aiding boats, crewed and captained by private adventurers given licence to act as they please upon the waves so long as they leave Bretonnian shipping unmolested. The Bretonnians call these captains privateers, though the captains of other nations see them as nothing less than pirates. 

## **Imperial Sailors**
The Empire does not have a grand tradition of seafaring. Emperor Hasso instituted the first of the Sea Lords in 632 IC, but the navy they oversaw was not a great fleet capable of exploration and conquest. It was a defensive force employed to protect the people of the Empire’s northern shore from Norse raiding. In later years, the development of the Empire’s navy was stymied by the protracted periods of civil strife and disunity between the provinces, and later the growth of an effective fleet was checked by the independence of Marienburg, which saw the greatest of the Empire’s naval forces confined to its rivers. 

## **Sailor[-] Priest of Manann** Human
_You bring the will of Manann to his followers and intercede to court his favour and avoid his wrath._ 

Priests of Manann are found working and ministering on board vessels as often as they are found in his temples and shrines. Manann is a fickle and moody deity, but he seems to respect a degree of practical ability and experience of the seas in his priests, and most of them spend a part of their career at sea. 

_‘They’re a rough crew alright, with salt in their beard and rope burns on their hands. But they’re always there when you need them, facing the waves and shouting prayers to the winds.’_ — Baron von Wolder, Ostland noble 

_‘He’s a moody sod, is Father Tangbart. Always jumping on us for little things like whistling or scratching your arse on the wrong day. Still, we put up with ‘im because we all want to come back with full nets and none drowned.’_ — Edla Weiss, Fisherwoman

## **Wave Lord — Gold 2**
**Skills:** Language (Any), Lore (Politics)

**Talents:** Chanty, Inspiring, Pure Soul, Seasoned Traveller

**Trappings:** Flotilla of Ships, Holy Relic, Subordinate High Priests 

Those who minister for Manann are drawn to their calling by a deep affinity for the god and a profound respect for the sea. The people who live by the whims of wave and storm look to their priests to beseech the capricious Lord of the Oceans for clemency and bring them protection from his moods. 

Most Priests come from coastal or river communities where the Cult is part of daily life. A minority are born inland and feel drawn to the sea by a strange pull, as if their destiny was always to venerate Manann. Settled Priests minister to sailors in port and local congregations where followers are prevalent. Others sail with merchant fleets, explorers, and naval vessels as a valued member of the crew. 

## **Initiates**
An Initiate of Manann accompanies a Priest, learning from them by observation, listening to their stories, and performing an endless, exhausting list of chores in the temple or on board a ship. They do little formal learning, and face continuous questioning by their Priest to sharpen their understanding of Manann and his cult. When they are deemed ready for ordination, the Initiate undergoes an ordeal where they show their face to Manann for his judgement. This involves exposure to the ferocity of the sea, storm, or flood, such as spending the night on a wave-lashed rock or enduring a stormy journey strapped to the mast of a small boat. 

Once ordained, the daily life of a settled Priest involves leading prayers in a temple, on board ships, or at the water’s edge. They bless ships heading out to sea and sanctify new vessels. Other Priests spend their lives travelling on ships and from port to port, tending to the spiritual needs of the crews and nautical types around them. There are also Warrior Priests of Manann (see **WFRP** , page 116) attached to a ship’s company and other nautical fighters. 

## **Vestments**
Priests wear robes in blue-green, turquoise, or some other colour reminiscent of water, trimmed with white wave patterns. They wear talismans shaped like shells, fish, seabirds, anchors, and Manann’s crown, along with scrimshawed bones and other maritime gewgaws. Strapping ship’s paraphernalia and bits of sea creature to yourself is a favoured sartorial choice. 

High Priests and Wave Lords oversee major cult centres or naval or mercantile fleets. Within the nautical sphere they are powerful individuals in their own right and relatively independent from one another. 

## **Priests of Manann on Board a Ship**
A Priest of Manann is a great asset to a crew. They lead prayers at each watch, implore their god to favour the vessel, and ensure the crew show him respect. Several times a week they deliver sermons from the poop deck or crow’s nest, leading hymns and accompanying the Chantyman in their songs. 

They also perform rituals to mark the passing of time, significant landmarks on a journey, or to influence the weather. A Priest of Manann can bring improvement to Manann’s Mood (page 130). 

A Priest of Manann should always get involved when it’s all hands on deck. Most are former sailors, so sailing and rowing comes naturally to them. That said, a captain wouldn’t usually expect a Priest to swab the deck or perform truly menial tasks. 

During difficult times, a Priest of Manann might command or discipline the crew on behalf of the captain, to stave off mutiny or bring unruly sailors in line. For an unpopular captain, it can be more effective and less risky to put the fear of Manann into an unsettled crew. 

## **Ship’s Gunner**
Dwarf, Halfling, High Elf, Human 

_You maintain and fire the guns aboard ship and are expert in their use._ 

The Ship’s Gunner is part of the crew, and just like any other crew member they are expected to help with the sailing of their vessel and to put their hand to anything involved in running the ship. In addition, they are experts on blackpowder weapons and their use at sea. 

_‘We’re not on land, now, are we? Feel this? We’re moving, up and down, side to side, and across the sea. See them? They’re moving, up and down, side to side, and across the sea in a different direction. Just because you can hit something on land, where nobody’s moving, doesn’t mean you’ll be able to hit a thing here, except maybe the sea, if you’re lucky.’_ 

— Uwe Eenkhoorn, Ship’s Gunner 

_‘Don’t take your match to the powder store.’_ — The first thing Powder Monkeys are taught

## **Master Gunner – Gold 1**
**Skills:** Charm, Lore (Oceans) 

**Talents:** Accurate Shot, Inspiring, Seasoned Traveller, Stout-hearted 

**Trappings:** Cabin, Quality Uniform 

This is a highly skilled and respected position, and as a Gunner rises in rank they find themself positioned above the main crew and treated more like an officer. As the Imperial Navy’s ships seem to be ever increasing in size and firepower, Gunners are increasingly sought after. And with rampant piracy on the Sea of Claws, merchant vessels are increasingly turning to guns to keep freebooters at bay. 

During sailing, the Ship’s Gunner is often treated as just another member of the crew; they are likely to be swabbing the deck or climbing the rigging like any other deckhand. Once battle is joined, however, they come into their own in their vital niche. 

## **Powder Monkeys**
A Powder Monkey’s role is to fetch blackpowder from the powder store deep within the ship’s hold and bring it to their gun. This arrangement keeps the blackpowder safe from fire but depends on quick, reliable Powder Monkeys. Powder Monkeys are generally children who take advantage of their smaller stature to dodge about the ship and duck out of the way of enemy fire. They are often sold to the navy for a pittance by the impoverished families of waterside slums for the chance of a better life. 

They are therefore largely uneducated and learn whatever they know during formative years aboard ship. With no other skills, they often spend all their lives as part of the ship’s crew. The brightest graduate to Ship’s Gunner, while others can take on different roles aboard ship. 

While Powder Monkeys have little status and are treated as fetchers and carriers by all the crew, the Ship’s Gunner is a more prestigious position. Once they have earned the right to specialise in operating their guns, they often manage to be exempted from the more mundane jobs in the daily running of the ship, concentrating instead on keeping their own station shipshape. A good Gunner still shows willingness to lend their hand to other chores when needed, however, if only to keep on good terms with the rest of the crew. 

## High Elf Gunners
High Elf ships routinely incorporate banks of repeating Eagle Claw Bolt Throwers. Although High Elves disdain to use blackpowder weaponry, they do have artillery crew on board their vessels who perform an equivalent task to Gunners. High Elves in this career have access to the Ranged (Crossbow) Skill rather than the Ranged (Blackpowder) Skill. 

## **’ Ship S Gunners**
The Ship’s Gunner is a skilled position. Maintaining the tackle and lines and loading the gun quickly to keep up a good rate of fire is vital to successful navy tactics. The expertise and experience required to know just when to fire the guns, especially on choppy seas, is something that, they say, can’t be taught. 

## **Gunnery Captains**
A Gunnery Captain oversees their own gun and their own small crew. Depending on the size of the gun this could be as many as six or eight people. In the heat of battle, deckhands and other crew are often roped in to man the guns in non-specialist roles, too. Experienced Gunnery Captains will often have several guns under their command. 

## **Master Gunners**
Master Gunners oversee every gun on board their vessel, and on military ships are often second in status only to the captain. Every Imperial Navy vessel has a Master Gunner, but because of their status it is not uncommon that these are brought in from other roles as an honorary position, and are Master Gunners in name only. 

The Ship’s Gunner who has served their time and risen in rank all the way from Powder Monkey is likely to resent this high-handed treatment, but would be wise not to make a show of it. 

## **Wrecker**
Dwarf, Human, Wood Elf 

_You lure vessels to a watery doom and make off with their precious cargo._ 

Bands of wreckers work around the coasts of all the nations of the Old World. They live by salvaging cargos from stricken vessels. Although there are some wreckers who live by treacherous lengths of coastline and wait patiently for ships to run aground, they may even manage to keep on the right side of the law as they do so, informing the authorities of their actions but seeking a cut of the salvage. But such people are not archetypal wreckers. The enterprise of wrecking is usually an opportunistic and criminal one, and the name is associated with those who take an active role in ensuring a steady supply of ships to wreck and plunder.

_‘In the distant past there was a dastardly Sartosan master who sailed several seas in his mighty galley. He cried “Avast! Avast me hearties!” he cried at last. “We’ll bring nasty merchants to their knees and seize vast hordes of booties ‘n’ rubies.” His crew, being ghastly, they all agreed.’_ — _Redhand’s Chanty_ , first verse 

## **False Pilots**
Some wreckers pose as huffers or pilots, promising to lead their victims safely past hazards, before directing them onto rocks or sandbanks. These wreckers will need to be convincing and charming enough to win captains into their confidence, as well as possessing enough of the skills of a true navigator to keep themselves safe as they ensure the doom of the ships that follow them. 

## **Luring Lights**
Some wreckers station themselves on islands or headlands near stretches of water where a ship’s lookout might expect to glimpse the signal from a lighthouse. By obscuring the light, or setting up their own false signals, the wreckers hope to guide ships onto hazards and then descend on the wreck to recover cargo. 

## **Sea Monsters**
Some wreckers may pursue rumours of a sea monster, finding its lair and waiting for it to venture forth and attack a vessel. Particularly brave wreckers may figure out a way to goad the creature into action. 

## **Piracy**
The most effective way of ensuring that a vulnerable ship falls into the grasp of wreckers is for them to take to the waves and wreck it themselves. 

There is no sharp dividing line between wreckers and pirates — to the authorities they are one and same. All wreckers need to be prepared to commit violence, for even those battered and bedraggled crew who manage to survive their ship being dashed to pieces may yet fight to defend their cargo and exact vengeance on those who conspired to exploit their misfortune. 

But pirates are usually those who have command of their own armed vessel, or even a small flotilla, and use it to launch attacks on merchant ships. 

Pirates constitute a diplomatic threat as well as a criminal one. If a landowner neglects to deal with a gang of pirates operating on his shores, they will soon be assumed to be acting in collusion with them. Due to the profits lost to piracy, efforts to catch and execute pirate crews can be unusual in the degree of otherwise hostile nations to cooperate and share resources. Most professional pirates either learn to operate far from civilisation or garner themselves a degree of legitimacy by finding someone willing to sponsor them as privateers. 

## The Sartosan Code
Pirates and wreckers operate outside of the law of their home nations, but their societies are not mere anarchies. Most pirates adopt a code common to the island of Sartosa. Pirates do not all abide by the code, but most learn about it, if only to preserve their own hide. 

The code combines macho notions of honour and integrity with a respect for might makes right. It is unwritten, but its values are espoused in the taverns and vice dens patronised by pirates. 

- All shall obey orders from their officers. 

- A crew member has the right to defend themself and their honour. 

- A crew member can challenge another to a fair duel, but the challenged gets choice of weapons. No person may interfere in this duel until one participant dies or yields. 

- Booty will be shared out as follows: 1 share to every sailor; 2 shares to the master carpenter, boatswain, and gunner; 10 shares to the captain. 

- Anyone who shirks from swabbing the decks or maintaining their weaponry will lose their share. 

- Anyone attempting to desert will be marooned. 

- A crewman striking another without warrant will recieve 10 lashes of the cat. 

- Everyone may vote on every important decision. 

- Everyone may have a share of captured vittles. 

- Anyone found stealing from another member of the crew will have their ears and nose slit open and be set ashore. 

- Crews members are sworn to serve upon the ship until each of them has made 100 GC. 

- No crewmember may fraternize with those who practice sorcery or worship the gods of Chaos.
